articles.headline: Meta's Multi-Stage Ads Ranking System Scales on User Sequence Learning
articles.body: Meta has published new research detailing the multi-stage architecture powering its ads ranking system that processes billions of daily user interactions across its platform. Rather than relying on manually engineered sparse features, Meta's approach focuses on modeling user sequences—the order and timing of actions users take across products, ads, and content—to capture genuine preferences and intent signals. This shift from static feature engineering to temporal sequence learning represents a fundamental change in how recommendations are ranked at scale. The system is designed to handle Meta's massive traffic volume while improving relevance and click-through rates by understanding not just what users do, but when and in what order they do it. Meta previously published work in 2024 on sequence learning for ads recommendations, and this new research builds on those foundations by showing how these learnings translate into production-grade scaling laws and multi-stage ranking pipelines. The architecture demonstrates how deep learning on user behavior sequences outperforms traditional sparse feature approaches, particularly in capturing nuanced preference signals that affect ad performance and user engagement.

This marks a shift from AI as a copilot (where humans make final decisions) to AI as an operator (where AI makes decisions within defined parameters). The capabilities unlocked by agentic AI include automating customer service resolution, executing data analysis workflows, generating and testing code across multiple iterations, and orchestrating business processes that previously required manual coordination across teams. OpenAI's findings suggest that enterprises using ChatGPT's extended thinking and code generation abilities are now building custom agents on top of these models, dramatically increasing throughput on knowledge work. The competitive advantage gap is widening: companies deploying agentic AI are seeing faster execution cycles, reduced manual oversight, and the ability to scale operations without proportional headcount increases. Context matters here—this is not fully autonomous AI replacing humans entirely, but rather AI systems that operate within guardrails and escalate to humans when needed, creating a hybrid execution model.

articles.hook: Google just built an AI doctor that actually listens to patients.
articles.headline: Google's AMIE AI Conducts Real-Time Clinical Video Consultations
articles.body: Google has unveiled AMIE (Automated Medical Intelligence Expert), a research medical AI system capable of conducting real-time clinical video consultations in simulated settings. AMIE represents a significant step toward AI-assisted healthcare delivery by demonstrating the ability to engage in live patient interactions through video, ask clarifying questions, listen to patient concerns, and provide clinical reasoning in real-time—capabilities that previously existed only in theoretical research. The system was tested in a first-of-its-kind study where AMIE participated in simulated clinical encounters, showing it can handle the nuanced, conversational nature of medical consultations rather than simply processing static data. Unlike previous medical AI systems that analyze lab results or imaging after the fact, AMIE operates dynamically during the consultation itself, requiring it to process audio, video, and conversational context simultaneously. The research demonstrates that AI can move beyond diagnostic support tools into the realm of patient-facing consultation, though Google emphasizes this is still in research phase and not yet deployed clinically. The implications are substantial: this could eventually reduce physician workload for routine consultations, extend access to preliminary medical advice in underserved regions, and create a new category of AI-assisted telehealth. However, critical questions remain about liability, regulatory approval, and whether patients would trust AI-led consultations without physician oversight.
examples: Watch AMIE engage a patient in real-time video, asking follow-up questions and taking detailed notes.
AMIE listens to a patient describe symptoms and provides preliminary clinical assessment live.
The AI handles interruptions and natural conversation flow—not reading a script.
articles.build: Telehealth platforms and medical practices can integrate AI consultation pre-screening: charge $15-40 per initial AI consultation (handling intake and basic triage), then route complex cases to physicians at premium rates. Medical coding and documentation services are hiring AI trainers at $35-65/hour to build datasets like AMIE's; companies like Nuance and ambient.ai are actively acquiring this talent. Healthcare startups building on Google's research can launch white-label telemedicine products within 6-12 months, targeting clinics at $500-2,000/month licensing fees.

articles.headline: Google's massive free AI agents course just hit 353k learners
articles.body: Google and Kaggle launched an AI Agents Intensive course designed to teach hundreds of thousands of people how to build and deploy AI agents—the next frontier in artificial intelligence. The course is completely free, making advanced AI agent development accessible to a massive global audience rather than limiting it to a select few. Google positioned this as a critical educational moment, recognizing that AI agents represent a major shift in how AI systems will work: moving from static models to systems that can take actions, make decisions, and operate autonomously. The course covers the full lifecycle—from conceptualizing agents to building them with Google's tools and frameworks, then deploying them into production environments. With 353,000 enrolled learners, this represents one of the largest coordinated pushes to democratize AI development skills. The no-cost model signals Google's strategy to build a massive developer base comfortable building on its AI infrastructure, creating a pipeline of professionals and entrepreneurs who will default to Google's tools when monetizing AI agents.
